passage: Throughout evolutionary history, human survival depended on navigating immediate physical threats such as predators, sudden storms, and food scarcity. Consequently, the human brain developed an acute sensitivity to urgent, visible dangers while remaining largely indifferent to gradual, long-term shifts. Psychologists call this tendency 'shifting baseline syndrome'—a phenomenon in which each generation accepts the degraded environmental or social conditions they grow up with as normal. Because ecological decline, climate warming, or soil depletion unfolds incrementally over decades rather than overnight, our perceptual systems fail to trigger an alarm. Overcoming this cognitive blind spot requires deliberately anchoring our decisions in long-term historical data and scientific benchmarks rather than relying solely on personal memory or short-term intuition.
